title: Many-Body Protection of Topological Edge Memory in Strong Interacting Quenches
authors: Yuxiao Hang, Stephan Haas, Rishabh Jha
abstract: Quantum quenches drive edge states far from equilibrium, yet whether the memory of a topological initial state survives in a non-integrable, interacting system has remained largely unexplored. We study this question in the bond-alternating XXZ chain -- an interacting Su--Schrieffer--Heeger model hosting symmetry-protected topological edge modes with markedly enhanced boundary magnetization -- and analyze quenches across all combinations of single-particle and many-body initial and final Hamiltonians. The results organize by a single distinction as we rigorously establish in this work: whether the post-quench Hamiltonian is free or genuinely interacting. For a free post-quench Hamiltonian, the dynamics is solved exactly by a correlation-matrix approach; the boundary-mode return amplitude decays as $t^{-3/2}$, and initial interactions enter only through a dressed one-body density matrix. For a genuinely interacting post-quench Hamiltonian, finite-time stability bounds prove that away from local resonances the first-dimer magnetization remains stable on time windows growing as arbitrarily large powers of the inverse inter-dimer coupling. Matrix product state simulations across all four protocols show that interactions in the final Hamiltonian markedly extend finite-time boundary memory -- with local suppression near the isotropic $SU(2)$ point -- revealing a many-body protection mechanism in a non-integrable system where scrambling would otherwise wash out initial-state memory fast.
summary: The paper explores how topological memory survives when a quantum system undergoes a quench into an interacting environment. By comparing single-particle and many-body evolution regimes, the authors rigorously prove that interactions actively protect this boundary memory over extended time scales. This reveals a fundamental 'many-body protection mechanism' in non-integrable systems.
main_problem: The study investigates whether topological memory encoded in an initial quantum state survives non-equilibrium evolution (quantum quenches) within strongly interacting, non-integrable many-body systems.
main_result: Interactions in the final Hamiltonian provide a 'many-body protection mechanism,' markedly extending the finite-time retention of boundary topological memory beyond what is predicted by free or single-particle dynamics.
method: The analysis combines exact analytical solutions for non-interacting limits (using correlation matrices) with deriving finite-time stability bounds and employing perturbative techniques to construct dressed, approximately conserved operators in interacting regimes.
model_or_system: The system is a bond-alternating XXZ spin chain modeled by an SSH-like Hamiltonian. Quenches are analyzed from a topologically non-trivial initial state ($\delta_i < 0$) to various final states ($\delta_f$), covering both free and genuinely interacting post-quench Hamiltonians.
key_observables: Topological boundary memory, specifically the first-dimer magnetization $\langle S_{z1} angle$, and the boundary-mode return amplitude $A_L(t)$.
important_parameters: The distinction between free vs. genuinely interacting post-quench Hamiltonians; the dimerization parameter ($\delta$); and the small coupling strength ($\epsilon$) used in perturbative analysis.
main_assumptions: The structure of the study is fundamentally organized around classifying the quench based on whether the final Hamiltonian ($H_f$) is free (quadratic) or genuinely interacting (many-body).
figures_summary: Figures benchmark the boundary-mode return amplitude decay, showing $t^{-3/2}$ for free dynamics. Other figures compare numerical results against analytical bounds derived from perturbative corrections to conserved charges.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes four quench protocols (SP$	o$SP, MB$	o$SP, SP$	o$MB, MB$	o$MB), first establishing exact results for the non-interacting case ($J_z=0$) and then using stability bounds and dressed operator constructions to prove memory retention in the interacting many-body limit.
why_interesting: This work provides rigorous analytical proof of topological protection mechanisms in strongly correlated, non-integrable systems far from equilibrium, which is a major frontier in quantum dynamics research relevant to condensed matter theory.
